---
title: "Outline"
subtitle: "Six chapters, in the order they will be taught"
---

The course is organised into six chapters. The first two explore why insurance exists and how insurance contracts are designed. The middle chapters turn to pricing and aggregate-loss modelling, while the final two focus on risk measurement and dependence between risks.

::: {.syllabus}

1. ### The history of insurance and the role of mathematics

   A brief history of insurance, from early forms of risk sharing in Antiquity to the emergence of modern insurance markets. We will discuss the development of marine insurance and the gradual separation of insurance from credit and trade finance in the late Middle Ages; the rise of Lloyd's; the Great Fire of London and the development of fire insurance; the rationalisation of life insurance; and the emergence of the modern insurance industry. Along the way, we will draw parallels with developments in probability and statistics, from Pascal and Fermat to the law of large numbers and actuarial science, and introduce some of the mathematicians and scientists who played an important part in the history of insurance.

2. ### The microeconomics of insurance

   Expected utility and risk aversion; the demand for insurance and its dependence on wealth; Mossin's model; and the optimality of deductible contracts. We conclude with two central problems of insurance markets under asymmetric information: adverse selection and moral hazard.
